case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed transfer of a termination proceeding from state juvenile court to the Turtle Mountain Tribal Court under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(b), holding the county failed to carry its burden of showing good cause to deny transfer and that applying ICWA to the child was not unconstitutional.
key_cases.relevance: Governs ICWA transfer motions: absent parental objection, the state court must transfer unless the opposing party proves good cause not to.
key_cases.quote: The burden of establishing good cause to deny a transfer is upon the party opposing the transfer.

key_cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that 'domicile' under ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law and that twins born off-reservation to parents domiciled on the reservation were themselves domiciled there, so the tribal court had exclusive jurisdiction and the state-court adoption decree had to be vacated.
key_cases.relevance: Controls the threshold jurisdictional question whenever an Indian child's domicile may place the case in tribal court under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a).
key_cases.quote: We therefore think it beyond dispute that Congress intended a uniform federal law of domicile for the ICWA.

key_cases.holding: Clear and convincing evidence supported the state-law grounds and the finding that active efforts had been made and failed, but because nothing in the record satisfied ICWA's requirement of proof beyond a reasonable doubt including qualified expert witness testimony, the court retained jurisdiction and remanded for a hearing limited to that ICWA requirement.
key_cases.relevance: States North Dakota's dual burden of proof whenever the child is an Indian child, tying state deprivation proof to ICWA's added federal proof.
key_cases.quote: When Indian children are involved in proceedings such as this, state and federal law create a dual burden of proof for the party seeking termination of parental rights.

key_cases.holding: Because the juvenile court's order contained inconsistent findings about whether ICWA applied and whether active efforts and the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt serious-damage element were established, the Supreme Court retained jurisdiction and remanded for clear findings before any termination could stand.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that a juvenile court must make explicit, internally consistent findings that ICWA (and N.D.C.C. ch. 27-20.3-19, North Dakota's codification) applies before proceeding on an Indian child.
key_cases.quote: Without consistent and clear factual findings supporting the application of ICWA and North Dakota heightened review for Indian families we are unable to determine the remaining issues raised by A.L.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights, holding incarceration alone does not prove abandonment but prognostic evidence of a long-continuing inability to care for the children satisfied both the state clear-and-convincing standard and ICWA's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt requirement.
key_cases.relevance: Applies ICWA's dual burden where the children are tribal members, requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt of likely serious emotional or physical damage.
key_cases.quote: While incarceration, by itself, does not establish abandonment of a child for purposes of terminating parental rights

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of a mother's rights to her Yankton Sioux daughter, holding that state and federal law impose a dual burden — the state statutory elements by clear and convincing evidence and ICWA's serious-damage element beyond a reasonable doubt — and holding for the first time that ICWA's active-efforts requirement under 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d) need be proven only by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: This is the source decision, relied on by both T.F. and K.S.D., that first stated North Dakota's ICWA dual burden of proof once a case involves an Indian child, and it also sets the standard for qualified expert witnesses where no cultural bias is implicated.
key_cases.quote: These state and federal provisions create a dual burden of proof for the party seeking parental termination of the parent of an Indian child

key_cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of C.D.
key_cases.holding: Reversing the dismissal of a stepmother's termination petition, the court held that although an Indian tribe's determination of its own membership and eligibility is binding and conclusive on the state court, the party asserting ICWA must produce admissible evidence of that determination, and allegations in the tribe's motions plus proof of Indian heritage and a pending enrollment application did not establish that the child was an Indian child.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the threshold question in every North Dakota ICWA case: the court must first find on admissible evidence that the child is an 'Indian child' under 25 U.S.C. § 1903(4), and the burden of producing that evidence falls on the party asserting ICWA's application.
key_cases.quote: An Indian tribe's determinations of its own membership and eligibility for membership are binding and conclusive in an ICWA proceeding.

key_cases.holding: The court retained jurisdiction and remanded for detailed ICWA findings, holding that while a qualified expert witness's preference against termination does not itself bar termination, the juvenile court's vague paraphrase of the statutory language was not the specific finding, beyond a reasonable doubt, that continued parental custody was likely to result in serious emotional or physical damage that 25 U.S.C. § 1912(f) requires.
key_cases.relevance: The most current North Dakota authority on the qualified-expert-witness element of ICWA: the ultimate serious-damage finding belongs to the judge, not the expert, but the court must make it explicitly and will not have it inferred from a vague reference to the statute.
key_cases.quote: A qualified expert witness's expressed preference to deny termination of parental rights does not preclude the court from making findings sufficient to satisfy ICWA and ordering termination.

key_cases.holding: On return from its own remand, the court affirmed the juvenile court's order denying the petition to terminate the mother's parental rights and instead removing the children from her custody for nine months, deferring to the finding that the qualified expert's testimony raised a reasonable doubt whether continued custody was likely to cause serious emotional or physical damage.
key_cases.relevance: The sequel that shows how ICWA's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard actually operates on remand: contrary expert testimony from the tribe's qualified expert can defeat the State's proof even where the court doubts the expert's assessment.
key_cases.quote: A finding relating to a likelihood of future harm requires some prognostic evidence providing "the basis for a reasonable prediction as to future action."

state_agency.name: North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services
state_agency.hotline: 1-833-958-3500 (8 a.m.-5 p.m. Central / 7 a.m.-4 p.m. Mountain, Mon-Fri; if a child is in immediate danger call 911)

mandatory_reporters: Listed professionals only — North Dakota is not a universal-reporting state (N.D. Cent. Code § 50-25.1-03(1))
Tier 1, 2, 3, and 4 mental health professionals (as defined in N.D. Cent. Code § 25-01-01) and any other medical or mental health professional
Religious practitioners of the healing arts
Schoolteachers, school administrators, and school counselors
Child care workers and child care licensors
Juvenile court personnel and probation officers
Licensed social workers and family service specialists
Members of the clergy, except when the knowledge is derived from information received as a spiritual adviser
Any person who discovers images of sexual conduct by a child on a workplace computer (N.D. Cent. Code § 50-25.1-03(3))
reporting_details: North Dakota is not a universal-reporting state: the professionals listed in N.D. Cent. Code § 50-25.1-03(1) must immediately report orally or in writing to the Department of Health and Human Services or its authorized agent, while any other person may report (N.D. Cent. Code §§ 50-25.1-03(2), 50-25.1-04(1)).

other: A child placed for care or adoption in violation of law

timeline_requirements.deadline: Immediately if there is a serious threat to the child's life or health; otherwise within department-set time frames

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: An extension of time must be requested of and granted by the department (N.D. Admin. Code § 75-03-19-04).
